110.0.0.en: "The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool."

110.0.1.en: 1- "The LORD said unto my Lord" declares that the Lord the Father speaks to "my Lord," who is the Son, Jesus Christ.

110.0.2.en: That King David calls Christ "my Lord" confirms the divinity of Christ, for David was a great king, and who could be the one he calls "my Lord," that is, his master, except God?

110.0.3.en: 2- In the Hebrew original of this psalm the word "LORD" is "Yahweh" and "my Lord" is "Adonai."

110.0.4.en: Yahweh is the name of God the Father in the Old Testament (Ex 6:3), and Adonai means Lord, or Master, and this is the name of Christ by which He was addressed on earth. This confirms that the verse tells us of a dialogue between the Father and the Son.

110.0.5.en: 3- This verse was fulfilled after Christ died on the cross, paid the wages of men's sins, and bound Satan. For after He completed the redemption, the Father calls the Son within the Godhead, to show His glory by His sitting at the right hand of the Father, that is, to show the fullness of His power and divinity, which appeared to men in His resurrection. By this He shows His authority over the demons, His enemies, and also over their wicked followers who crucified Christ and insulted Him, and who submitted to Him and declared their faith in Him, like Longinus who pierced Him with the spear.

110.0.6.en: 4- We cannot understand the equality of the Son with the Father in essence except by the Holy Spirit; it is the Spirit who revealed this truth to David (Mt 22:43). And because of this equality, the sitting of the Son at the right hand of the Father, that is, the declaration of His equality with the Father because they are one in essence, is an equality that is constant from eternity to eternity. Although it was hidden from the eyes of men in the Incarnation of Christ, His sufferings and His death, the Holy Spirit declares it to David and to all believers, especially after He showed His power in His resurrection.

110.0.7.en: 5- The sitting of the Son at the right hand of the Father is the sitting of Christ, God incarnate, that is, in His divinity and His humanity, to reign forever, triumphant over His enemies the demons. By this He declares to all humanity that believes in Him that He gives it authority and victory over all the wars of the demons, through Him and by His power.

110.0.8.en: And after humanity completes its striving on earth, the triumphant Christ grants it to ascend to heaven to live with Him forever, and to enter through the closed doors, the doors of the Kingdom, so that He permits humanity that believes in Him to enter and live in heaven.

110.1.0.en: "The LORD shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies."

110.1.1.en: 1- The rod is the rod of the king, and this appeared on the cross, for Christ reigned from a tree (the psalm of the Ninth Hour of the Agpeya: "The Lord hath reigned from the tree").

110.1.2.en: 2- If the first verse showed a dialogue between the Father and the Son, this verse completes for us the work of the Trinity, for it tells us of the work of the Holy Spirit, who sends out the preaching of Christ the King and Savior from Zion, that is, Jerusalem, to the whole world, that it may believe in the salvation of Christ.

110.1.3.en: 3- By the reign of Christ on the cross He rules over His enemies, that is, the wicked who opposed Christ and crucified Him. It says "rule," not "destroy," and this rule appears in two forms:

110.1.4.en: a - These wicked people believe in Christ and submit to Him.

110.1.5.en: b - They do not believe in Christ, but they fear Him, so He restrains their evil from harming His children except to the extent that He sees to be for their benefit.

110.2.0.en: "Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power, in the beauties of holiness from the womb of the morning: thou hast the dew of thy youth."

110.2.1.en: "Willing": it means that they are volunteers and have come to the Lord of their own freedom.

110.2.2.en: 1- "Thy people shall be willing": the Father addresses the Son, saying that He offered salvation on the cross and many believed in Him, and these are His people. They submitted to Him of their own freedom, and even went out preaching in His name to the whole world. In the Septuagint translation, in the Agpeya, it says "With thee is the principality," that is, thy people of their own freedom submitted to thy lordship in their faith and their preaching.

110.2.3.en: 2- "In the day of thy power": the day of Christ's power is the day of the cross, on which He gave salvation to His people, and the day of salvation extended through the life of the believers throughout their lives, so that they lived in the power of Christ, defeated the demons, stood firm in their faith, and walked in the virtues. In the Agpeya it says "in the day of thy strength," that is, thy power.

110.2.4.en: 3- "In the beauties of holiness": the beauties of holiness are the virtues with which the people of God adorn themselves, that is, they walk in the virtues they have acquired by the power of Christ, so that He is glorified in them. In the Agpeya it says "in the splendors of the saints," that is, the virtues of the saints, and so lived all the children of God.

110.2.5.en: 4- "From the womb of the morning": that is, before the dawn comes forth, and this tells us of the eternity of the Son, who became incarnate in the fullness of time. What takes place in the womb is hidden and secret, so the eternity of Christ is a mystery that rises above the mind, how He exists from eternity and became incarnate in the fullness of time, to shine like the dawn upon all who sit in darkness, enlightening by His salvation all who are subject to sin and death, and they are all mankind, and giving them His salvation that they may live anew.

110.2.6.en: - The birth of Christ from the womb before the dawn, besides signifying His eternity in His begetting from the Father and His equality with Him in essence, also signifies His birth in the fullness of time from the womb of the Virgin, and this actually took place at night before the dawn. In the Agpeya it says "before the morning star have I begotten thee," that is, before the sun and the moon the Son was begotten of the Father, because He is eternal and has the same nature. At the same time He was born of the Virgin at night before the morning star, that is, before the rising of the sun.

110.2.7.en: 5- "Thou hast the dew of thy youth": the dew is the moisture of the morning; Christ has the dew, and it means the many who believe in Him, who are like drops of dew falling from heaven. They are heavenly by their faith in Christ and their spiritual conduct. "Thy youth" means youthfulness, vitality and strength. The believers in the early Church, in the apostolic age, were full of vitality and of love for Christ.

110.2.8.en: And in every generation there are believers full of vitality.

110.2.9.en: May you live in spiritual youth, that is, take care of your prayers and your readings so that you feel Christ, and He gives you zeal and opens your heart with love for doing good and for loving every person, even the one who wrongs you.

110.3.0.en: "The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek."

110.3.1.en: 1- The psalm speaks here about Christ, and the Lord, that is, the Father, has sworn that Christ is the priest after the order of Melchizedek; that is, He is priest and king forever. Among the Jews the priesthood and the kingship were not joined in one tribe, for the priesthood was from the tribe of Levi and the kingship from the tribe of Judah. Yet David and his son Solomon, the kings, practiced the priesthood in part, for David put on the priestly garments when he brought the ark back to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:14).

110.3.2.en: 2- "The Lord hath sworn," for He alone has the right to swear, since He has complete power to fulfill what He swears by, whereas men are weak and cannot fulfill what they swear, so an oath is not fitting for them. And "will not repent" means that He will not go back on His word, because His command is protected and established forever, that Christ is priest and reigns forever. And if it is said of God that He repented, that is a divine expression for the possibility of God relenting from His word if man repents, as in the repentance of the people of Nineveh.

110.3.3.en: 3- The priesthood of Christ is eternal, therefore it says "after the order of Melchizedek," who is the king of Salem, that is, the king of peace, and of whom no beginning or end is known. The priesthood of Aaron, however, is given to limited men who die; the priesthood of Christ is after the rite of Melchizedek and not of Aaron.

110.3.4.en: We note that Melchizedek offered his sacrifice of bread and wine, as Christ did, and Melchizedek was a type of Christ (Gen 14:18).

110.4.0.en: 5- The Lord at thy right hand shall strike through kings in the day of his wrath. 6- He shall judge among the heathen, he shall fill the places with the dead bodies; he shall wound the heads over many countries.

110.4.2.en: 1- This verse shows the equality of the Father with the Son, for it says to the Son, "The Lord at thy right hand," as was mentioned in (v. 1) that the Son sits at the right hand of the Father; and the sitting at the right hand does not mean a place, because God is without limit and has no right or left. What is meant by the right hand is power and glory.

110.4.3.en: 2- The two verses show the authority of Christ, who strikes through, judges and crushes all who oppose Him, meaning the demons and all the wicked who follow them; for everyone who opposed God and His Church throughout the generations was broken and became humbled, like Nebuchadnezzar who became like the beasts (Dan 4:33), and Holofernes whom Judith killed (Jdt 13:10), and Antiochus the Great who was eaten by worms and died in the days of the Maccabees (2 Macc 9:9), and like Diocletian and the emperors who stood against the Church, and other kings of the earth who were broken, while the Church remained strong until now.

110.4.4.en: 3- The judgment of Satan was accomplished on the cross when Christ bound him by His death on the cross, and on the last day of judgment He will cast him into eternal torment, together with all the wicked who follow him.

110.5.0.en: "He shall drink of the brook in the way: therefore shall he lift up the head."

110.5.1.en: 1- Christ the Son drank from the river of sufferings, bore all the hardships of the cross, and died to redeem us, and by the power of His divinity He lifted up His head in the resurrection, to raise us up in Him from the death of sin.

110.5.2.en: 2- Every spiritual man in the hour of affliction drinks from the river of the Holy Spirit, to whom he flees for refuge, so his heart is comforted and he stands firm during the trial, so that at its end he lifts up his head by the power of God and triumphs over the wars of Satan.

110.5.3.en: When any affliction meets you, be sure that it is by God's permission for your good, so do not let your heart be troubled. But seek God in prayer and humility, offering repentance for your sins, and you will be purified, and God will lift up your head, glorify you and bless you with many blessings.

110.5.4.en: Thanksgiving to God the fortress "Alleluia. I will praise the LORD with my whole heart, in the assembly of the upright, and in the congregation" (v. 1) Introduction:

110.5.6.en: 2- When was it written? There is a title in the Septuagint translation of this psalm, which is "For the return of Haggai and Zechariah." So the time of its writing would be after the return from the captivity.

110.5.7.en: 3- This psalm speaks of the works of God, their greatness and their attributes, and it calls man to thank God and praise Him while remaining steadfast in faith in Him.

110.5.8.en: 4- There is a relation between this psalm and the one that follows it, in that the first speaks of the attributes of the works of God, while Psalm 112 speaks of the attributes of those who fear God.

110.5.9.en: 5- This psalm is liturgical, and it used to be chanted at the feast of the Passover, as St. Augustine tells us.

110.5.10.en: 6- This psalm and the one that follows are arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet. This psalm is divided into twenty-two parts (a verse may contain two or three parts), and each part begins with a letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It is noted that these two psalms contain verses similar to those in the books of Psalms and Proverbs.

110.5.11.en: 7- Because Psalm 110, which precedes this psalm, speaks of the Ascension of Christ, this psalm and the two psalms that follow it each begin with the word Alleluia. These three psalms express joy at the Ascension of Christ.

110.5.12.en: 8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, in which Christ died on the cross and completed our redemption; therefore we glorify the great works of God by which we obtained our salvation and redemption.

111.0.s.en: (1) Thanks to God for His works

111.0.0.en: "Praise ye the LORD. I will praise the LORD with my whole heart, in the assembly of the upright, and in the congregation."

111.0.1.en: 1- The psalm begins with rejoicing, praise and thanksgiving to God for all His benefits. This praise is from the whole heart, that is, with all the feelings, and not only with the tongue; that is, the whole being of the psalmist thanks God and praises Him, for he is not occupied with the desires of the world or its cares, but his only occupation is the praise of God. In this he fulfills God's commandment to love Him with all his heart (Deut 6:5).

111.0.2.en: 2- He is not content with thanksgiving and praise in his chamber, but also praises God in the assembly and congregation of the upright, that is, those who believe in God and are upright in His worship. He is encouraged, and encourages those around him, to praise God, and this confirms that this psalm is a liturgical psalm.

111.1.0.en: "The works of the LORD are great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein."

111.1.1.en: 1- The works of God are great and show the extent of His wisdom and power in creation, and in His ordering of the universe and keeping it in balance. Indeed His greatness appears also in making creatures act contrary to their nature for the glory of His name and for the salvation of His children; so He makes the fire not burn the three youths, and the hungry, ravening lions not harm Daniel. And on the contrary hail and fire come together to destroy the Egyptians, and the sun and the moon do not shine in the plague of darkness.

111.1.2.en: 2- The believers seek out the works of God; that is, they meditate on them and behold God their Creator, so their hearts are gladdened and they praise God for His greatness, and indeed they always seek to meditate on the works of God in order to discover the God hidden behind them, and to remain in constant glorification and praise of Him.

111.2.0.en: "His work is honourable and glorious: and his righteousness endureth for ever." Honourable: greatness.

111.2.3.en: 1- The works of God are very great and beautiful, not only in huge beings such as the sun and the moon, but in the smallest creatures, such as insects, or microbes invisible to the naked eye. All of them were created in wisdom and have an order in life that preserves them, however weak they appear or whatever conditions oppose them. All this God created for the sake of man; how much greater, then, is His work in creating man, caring for him, and ordering his life.

111.2.4.en: 2- God is perfect in His justice, and His justice is everlasting, but He is long-suffering toward the wicked to give them an opportunity to repent. Therefore man should not be disturbed if he suffers injustice, because God is just and will compensate him partly on earth and without limit in eternity. On the other hand, no one should rush to wrong another even if he has the opportunity. For God will surely punish him, whether in this life or, still more, in the next life if he refuses to repent.

111.3.0.en: "He hath made his wonderful works to be remembered: the LORD is gracious and full of compassion."

111.3.1.en: 1- It is important for man to remember the wonderful works of God, so that his faith may be strengthened and they may move him to praise and thanksgiving. Therefore God commanded His people to keep a portion of the manna in a pot inside the ark of the covenant throughout their lives, and also Aaron's rod that budded, and above all the tables of the commandments. And God commanded His people to sanctify days as feasts in which to remember God. And to this day the Church takes care to remember the works of God through the feasts and fasts, and above all through the living, tangible memorial of His Body and Blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist.

111.3.2.en: 2- Remembering the works of God reveals to the one who takes care to do so the graciousness and mercy of God, and by this those who thank God become attached to His person and love Him with all their hearts, so more abundant mercies overflow upon them, until they are filled with love and mercy toward others, and serve them and honor them.

111.3.3.en: May you set aside even a few minutes every day or every week to meditate on the works of God, whether in nature, or its ordering, or your creation, or His care for you, so that your heart may be calmed and filled with love for Him, and your tongue may be loosed to praise Him.

111.4.0.en: "He hath given meat unto them that fear him: he will ever be mindful of his covenant."

111.4.1.en: 1- God remembered His covenant with the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so He cared for His people in the wilderness of Sinai and gave them manna as food for forty years, because they believed in Him and feared Him. He fed them in a barren wilderness, the wilderness of Sinai, as He fed His children throughout the generations, such as Elijah, whom He fed by means of the raven (1 Kgs 6:17), and as Christ fed the multitudes with the two fish and the five loaves (Mt 14:13-21).

111.4.2.en: 2- The meat means the Passover, and therefore this psalm is chanted at the feast of the Passover, as we mentioned in the introduction. The Passover is a type of the sacrifice of Christ, that is, His Body and Blood, which He gives in His Church every day to those who fear Him as an everlasting covenant, that is, He feeds them spiritually forever. And God does not forget His covenant, and He wants His believing children also not to forget His covenant, so they partake of His Body and Blood always for the forgiveness of their sins, and that He may give them a strong spiritual life. Just as He commanded His people in the days of Moses to put manna in the golden pot inside the ark of the covenant, that they might always remember how He fed them, remembering His covenant with Abraham, so that they might rely on Him and thank Him.

111.5.0.en: "He hath shewed his people the power of his works, that he may give them the heritage of the heathen."

111.5.1.en: 1- God showed His people the children of Israel, who were enslaved in Egypt, the power of His works, not only by promises and words, but in deed, through the ten plagues, the dividing of the Red Sea and their crossing it, and the drowning of Pharaoh and all his army.

111.5.2.en: 2- After God sustained them in the wilderness of Sinai for forty years in a miraculous way, giving them water from the rock, manna from heaven, and also quail, and keeping their clothes and sandals from wearing out, and protecting them from enemies, so that they triumphed over them, such as Amalek, and finally brought them to a river and divided it so that they might cross over, then He destroyed the pagans who dwelt in Canaan because of their wickedness, and gave the children of Israel their land because of their faith in Him.

111.6.0.en: 7- The works of his hands are verity and judgment; all his commandments are sure. 8- They stand fast for ever and ever, and are done in truth and uprightness.

111.6.1.en: 1- The works of God are sure; that is, certain and true, meaning that they are for the good of man, and likewise all His commandments are steadfast; even if man does not understand them at the time and endures afflictions, he discovers in the end that the narrow gate and the hard way is what leads to eternal life. God is long-suffering toward evil, but He will surely reward those who do good.

111.6.2.en: 2- The commandments and works of God are steadfast and cannot change even if the whole world changes, and all of them are truths however much Satan tries to cast doubt on them. They alone are upright, and their opposite is deviation, however tempting the matter may be, like the desires of the world. Therefore the believer must hold fast to his faith and to God's commandments, and reject every doubt even if the words of Satan are convincing; for his deceit will be exposed after this.

111.7.0.en: "He sent redemption unto his people: he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend is his name."

111.7.1.en: 1- God sent redemption to His people Israel, who were enslaved in Egypt, so He freed them and brought them out of Egypt and across the Red Sea, and Pharaoh and all his army died in their place. And God established His covenant with His people, to be their God and to have them as His people, so He kept them and sustained them in the wilderness of Sinai, gave them the land of Canaan as a possession, and showed His holiness to them when He dwelt in His house in the tabernacle of meeting, after He had appeared in His might on the mountain, and the people offered Him sacrifices and feared Him and worshiped Him, so they enjoyed His care and His fellowship.

111.7.2.en: 2- All that God did with His people in the Old Testament was a type of the redemption of Christ on the cross, and then He established His covenant in His Church by the sacrament of the Eucharist. So the Holy One dwelt among His children and sanctified them by the Holy Myron and by partaking of His Body and Blood.

111.7.3.en: 3- The name of God is holy, for in it is all righteousness and goodness, and it is also reverend and fearful, and exceedingly great, and so it deserves glorification and praise. At the same time His name is very fearful to the wicked, especially on the day of judgment when He casts them into eternal torment.

111.8.0.en: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever."

111.8.1.en: 1- "The beginning of wisdom," that is, its start, its root and its first source, is the fear of the Lord, and there can be no wisdom without the fear of the Lord; for the fear keeps man away from evil and leads him to humility, so that he is able to behold God, who guides him in all his spiritual and material affairs.

111.8.2.en: 2- And wisdom is good not for him who knows it in theory, but for him who lives it, that is, carries out God's commandments and clings to Him, so he fears Him and loves Him and lives in peace.

111.8.3.en: 3- When man knows God through wisdom he rejoices greatly and praises Him continually. He keeps praising God throughout his life, and the praise even extends into eternity. So the psalm ends with praise as it began with it, with the word Alleluia. And although this verse is the close of this psalm, it is the beginning of the next psalm, which speaks of those who fear God.

111.8.4.en: If God has worked many works in your life that show His fatherhood and care, you must believe in Him, so that you live at ease, relying on Him, and your heart is free to love Him and praise Him, and you taste the sweetness of the Kingdom while you are still on earth.

111.8.5.en: The one who fears the Lord and loves others "Alleluia. Blessed is the man that feareth the LORD, that delighteth greatly in his commandments" (v. 1) Introduction:

111.8.6.en: 1- Its author: not mentioned, so it is one of the orphan psalms, and some attribute it to the prophet David.

111.8.8.en: Because there is a title for this psalm in the Septuagint translation, which is "For the return of Haggai and Zechariah"

111.8.9.en: its time of writing could be after the captivity, or in the days of David if David is its author.

111.8.10.en: 3- There is a similarity between this psalm and the one before it, that is (Ps 111); if the previous psalm blesses God and His works, this psalm blesses the one who fears God and shows his attributes and blessings.

111.8.11.en: 4- This psalm is considered one of the wisdom psalms, as appears from its beginning.

111.8.12.en: 5- This psalm, as we mentioned in the introduction to the previous psalm, is one of the psalms that begin with the word Alleluia, and it is among three psalms (Ps 111, 112, 113) full of the glorification of God who ascended into heaven, as Psalm 110, which precedes these three psalms, tells us.

111.8.13.en: 6- This psalm is divided into twenty-two parts and arranged according to the Hebrew alphabet, each part beginning with one of the letters of the alphabet in order, like the psalm before it.

111.8.14.en: 7- This psalm resembles the books of Proverbs and Psalms, for there are some verses common to them.

111.8.15.en: 8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Ninth Hour, in which Christ completed the redemption, and the Righteous One died on the cross for us sinners. This psalm tells us of Christ the Righteous One, whose righteousness endures forever.
